{{Short description|Type of pumping lemma}}
In [[computer science]], in particular in [[formal language theory]], the '''[[pumping lemma]] for context-free languages''', also known as the '''[[Yehoshua Bar-Hillel|Bar-Hillel]] lemma''',{{sfn|Kreowski|1979}} is a [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] that gives a property shared by all [[context-free language]]s and generalizes the [[pumping lemma for regular languages]].

The pumping lemma can be used to construct a [[refutation by contradiction]] that a specific language is ''not'' context-free. Conversely, the pumping lemma does not suffice to guarantee that a language ''is'' context-free; there are other necessary conditions, such as [[Ogden's lemma]], or the [[Interchange lemma]].

== Formal statement ==
{{Dark mode invert|[[File:Pumping lemma for context-free languages.svg|thumb|300px|Proof idea: If <math>s</math> is sufficiently long, its [[derivation tree]] w.r.t. a [[Chomsky normal form]] grammar must contain some [[context-free grammar#Formal definitions|nonterminal]] <math>N</math> twice on some [[tree path]] (upper picture). Repeating <math>n</math> times the derivation part <math>N</math> ⇒...⇒ <math>vNx</math> obtains a derivation for <math>uv^n wx^n y</math> (lower left and right picture for <math>n=0</math> and <math>2</math>, respectively).]]}}
If a language <math>L</math> is context-free, then there exists some integer <math>p \geq 1</math> (called a "pumping length"){{sfn|Berstel|Lauve|Reutenauer|Saliola|2009}} such that every string <math>s</math> in <math>L</math> that has a [[string length|length]] of <math>p</math> or more symbols (i.e. with <math>|s| \geq p</math>) can be written as

<math display=block>s = uvwxy</math>

with [[substring]]s <math>u, v, w, x</math> and <math>y</math>, such that

# <math>|vx| \geq 1</math>,
# <math>|vwx| \leq p</math>, and
# <math>uv^n wx^n y \in L</math> for all <math>n \geq 0</math>.

Below is a formal expression of the Pumping Lemma.

<math display=block>
\begin{array}{l}                                                                                                                                       
(\forall  L\subseteq \Sigma^*)  \\                                                                                                                     
\quad      (\mbox{context free}(L) \Rightarrow \\                                                                                                           
\quad      ((\exists p\geq 1) ((\forall s\in L) ((|s|\geq p) \Rightarrow \\                                                                           
\quad ((\exists u,v,w,x,y \in \Sigma^*) (s=uvwxy \land |vx|\geq 1 \land |vwx|\leq p \land (\forall n \geq 0)                                                              
(uv^nwx^ny\in L)))))))                                                                                                                   
\end{array} 
</math>

== Informal statement and explanation ==
The pumping lemma for context-free languages (called just "the pumping lemma" for the rest of this article) describes a property that all context-free languages are guaranteed to have.

The property holds for all strings in the language that are of length at least <math>p</math>, where <math>p</math> is a constant—called the ''pumping length''—that varies between context-free languages.

Say <math>s</math> is a string of length at least <math>p</math> that is in the language.

The pumping lemma states that <math>s</math> can be split into five substrings, <math>s = uvwxy</math>, where <math>vx</math> is non-empty and the length of <math>vwx</math> is at most <math>p</math>, such that repeating <math>v</math> and <math>x</math> the same number of times (<math>n</math>) in <math>s</math> produces a string that is still in the language.  It is often useful to repeat zero times, which removes <math>v</math> and <math>x</math> from the string (this is "pumping down"). This process of "pumping up" <math>s</math> with additional copies of <math>v</math> and <math>x</math> is what gives the pumping lemma its name.

[[Finite language]]s (which are regular and hence context-free) obey the pumping lemma trivially by having <math>p</math> equal to the maximum string length in <math>L</math> plus one. As there are no strings of this length the pumping lemma holds [[Vacuous truth|vacuously]].

== Usage of the lemma ==

The pumping lemma is often used to prove that a given language {{mvar|L}} is non-context-free, by showing that arbitrarily long strings {{mvar|s}} are in {{mvar|L}} that cannot be "pumped" without producing strings outside {{mvar|L}}.

For example, if <math>S\subset \N</math> is infinite but does not contain an (infinite) [[arithmetic progression]], then <math>L = \{a^{n} : n\in S\}</math> is not context-free. In particular, neither the [[prime number]]s nor the [[square number]]s are context-free.

For example, the language <math>L = \{ a^n b^n c^n | n > 0 \}</math> can be shown to be non-context-free by using the pumping lemma in a [[proof by contradiction]]. First, assume that {{mvar|L}} is context free. By the pumping lemma, there exists an integer {{mvar|p}} which is the pumping length of language {{mvar|L}}. Consider the string <math>s = a^p b^p c^p</math> in {{mvar|L}}. The pumping lemma tells us that {{mvar|s}} can be written in the form <math>s = uvwxy</math>, where {{mvar|u, v, w, x}}, and {{mvar|y}} are substrings, such that <math>|vx| \geq 1</math>, <math>|vwx| \leq p</math>, and <math>uv^i wx^i y \in L</math> for every integer <math>i \geq 0</math>. By the choice of {{mvar|s}} and the fact that <math>|vwx| \leq p</math>, it is easily seen that the substring {{mvar|vwx}} can contain no more than two distinct symbols. That is, we have one of five possibilities for {{mvar|vwx}}:

# <math>vwx = a^j</math> for some <math>j \leq p</math>.
# <math>vwx = a^j b^k</math> for some {{mvar|j}} and {{mvar|k}} with <math>j+k \leq p</math>
# <math>vwx = b^j</math> for some <math>j \leq p</math>.
# <math>vwx = b^j c^k</math> for some {{mvar|j}} and {{mvar|k}} with <math>j+k \leq p</math>.
# <math>vwx = c^j</math> for some <math>j \leq p</math>.

In each case, <math>uv^i wx^i y</math> does not contain equal numbers of each letter for any <math>i \neq 1</math>. Thus, <math>uv^2 wx^2 y</math> does not have the form <math>a^i b^i c^i</math>. This contradicts the definition of {{mvar|L}}. Therefore, our initial assumption that {{mvar|L}} is context free must be false.

In 1960, Scheinberg proved that <math>L = \{ a^n b^n a^n | n > 0 \}</math> is not context-free using a precursor of the pumping lemma.{{sfn|Scheinberg|1960|loc=Lemma 3, and its use on pp. 374-375}}

While the pumping lemma is often a useful tool to prove that a given language ''is not'' context-free, there are languages that are not context-free, but still satisfy the condition given by the pumping lemma, for example
<math display="block">L = \{ b^j c^k d^l | j, k, l \in \mathbb{N} \} \cup \{ a^i b^j c^j d^j | i, j \in \mathbb{N}, i \ge 1\}</math>
For <math>s = b^j c^k d^l</math> with e.g. <math>j \ge 1</math>, choose <math>vwx</math> to consist only of <math>b</math>'s, for <math>a^ib^jc^jd^j</math>, choose <math>vwx</math> to consist only of <math>a</math>'s. In both cases all pumped strings are still in <math>L</math>.{{sfn|Hopcroft|Ullman|1979| loc=sect.6.1|p=129}} 

To prove that a given language ''is'' context-free, it is sufficient to construct a [[pushdown automaton]] that accepts it.
